body:
> I see no urgent need for MinML to replace HTML as an "on-the-wire" syntax transmitted over HTTP connections. Rather, I see such a concise HTML syntax as something that website builders like Wordpress, Hugo, etc., as well as interactive text-entry systems (like GitHub issues) might support in addition to (or instead of) Markdown.

It does seem doubtful that new on-the-wire syntax would be considered worthwhile by vendors especially given the security concerns associated with HTML (not) round-tripping when serialized. But if this is not the objective anyway, what makes this a proposal exactly? Why would HTML be the place to define a new concrete syntax if HTML implementations aren’t meant to recognize it?

> Of course this is still at an early stage, and it remains to be seen whether MinML or something like it can prove "concise enough" or "attractive enough" in people's perceptions to make it a practical alternative to Markdown-style syntax. But at least starting this discussion is the main purpose of this post.

It might be interesting to see what shakes out of userland custom elements that implement alternative markup syntax. I’ve only seen the pattern of treating logical text content as input to map to output in a shadow tree used for (gracefully degrading) syntax highlighting elements to date, but the same pattern would seemingly serve alternative markup syntax pretty well. Converting alternative markup to HTML in advance would be better in the typical case, but scenarios can arise where that’s either not true or not possible, e.g. live editing widgets. Their usage might provide hints about adoption.

> All feedback is welcome.

I’ll bite and say I don’t think MinML constitutes an improvement. In particular I find it confusing that the two apparent syntactic constructs in the sequence `bee em[yoo] tiful [star]` — “bare words” and “bracketed words” let’s say — are used to denote three different things (respectively: chardata, tag name, chardata, chardata, character reference) depending on context. Whether and how much this seems confusing is subjective, but personally if I were seeking new markup syntax, avoiding this sort of “syntax overloading” would be a high priority.
